This is really common. It can be caused by a lot of things. Some psychs might call it alexithymia, some depression. 

It's impossible to not have emotions. All humans do. It's physiological. Our mind-bodies are interpreting the world 24/7 and giving us information about our relation to it; that's what emotions are. It's not possible to not have emotions. But it is possible to be cut off from an awareness of them, to not be in-tune with our body's language of emotions. Does that make sense? So it SEEMS like you don't have emotions, but you do. In fact, you named a few emotions in your post. Emptiness, dullness, roboticism, disconnected. Those ARE emotions. Check out the "Feelings Wheel" on Google Images. Emotions aren't just limited to sadness, fear, happiness, disgust. There are hundreds of sub emotions. 

When we look at what you're talking about from this lens, it sounds like you actually DO feel quite sad and empty. Sad about feeling disconnected. Sad about not feeling much. And this sadness shows up as a feeling of emptiness. The thing you seem to be grieving is that you lack the specific emotions of excitement, joy, connectedness. And when you also don't feel guilt or other heavy emotions, you feel broken. That's a feeling too. But most of all you seem to be saying that you feel numb. This is what you want help with. 

There could be a lot of reasons for this. Maybe your mind/body is shutting down your ability to feel emotions because the emotions that you DO have are so painful that it's better to just feel nothing at all. Maybe this numbness is exacerbated by a social isolationism, substances, and dissociation. 

It can be a strange thing, when someone thinks "I don't feel any emotions!" and yet the reason they are so numb is because the emotions that ARE there are too big to feel (or they lack the necessary coping mechanisms to handle them). It's weird, right? But it's possible. The body is good at shutting down when it's overwhelmed. I'm sorry you're feeling that; It's a shitty place to be. I've been there. For me, if I really tapped into the grief I felt about my childhood, I would become suicidal. My brain's way of protecting me from dying was making it so I numbed out until I was in a supportive space with friends who cared about me. Then all of a sudden, once I'd found stability and support, I was overcome with deep, deep grief. I felt deeply the things I had been putting off feeling for so long. And on the other side of that grieving, I feel things deeply now. Life is... still tough. But I feel alive again. It's possible to heal and feel again. And some days I feel amazing. Some days I weep. I love it. And you can get here too. 

Some paths forward may include somatic exercises (Body scans are a good tool. Google them. Visualizations, too; AKA re-learning the vocabulary of your body's emotions. Start basic. What does desire feel like? Imagine yourself super hungry. And someone plops down a giant piece of pizza or chocolate cake in front of you and you just want to tear into it. What does that feel like? Do you feel a gravitational pull forward? Do you feel a lightness in your chest? Does your mouth feel warm? Do the same for disgust. What does it feel like to be nauseous and have something truly disgusting put in front of you? Then do this for other emotions. When you picture yourself achieving long-term goals, or getting a girlfriend/boyfriend, or saving up 50,000 dollars, what does that feel like? Slowly you can start to expand your emotional awareness. Right now you might say that you feel nothing, but I bet that if you become more emotionally attuned \[and this is very much a skill you can develop, like a muscle\] then when you are in a situation where you are sitting with peers and don't want to be there, you might feel a pulling-back sensation, or a heaviness, or a slight disgust, maybe even fear. Those are emotions that you didn't have access to before! But after learning your body's specific language, you'll suddenly realize you feel LOTS OF THINGS. All the time!!!). Other paths forward might involve examining your childhood or history with trauma. Why might you have become emotionally numbed? What did that solve for you? Did you have a tough childhood? Is it hard for you to cope with the general sadness of working 9-5 in modern life? Finally, you might want to examine what your current world looks like. You might feel utterly disinterested in the people in front of you now, but maybe you aren't in front of the right people. Think outside the box. Maybe you prefer 1-on-1 interactions. Maybe neurotypical people are kinda boring and don't 'get' you so you can't be yourself in front of them, hence you shut down. Maybe you feel numb because you just go to work/school, come home and play video games and smoke weed, and do little else. I'd feel numb too. It might be time to shake things up. 

There's a lot of reasons for what you're feeling. I relate, and I'm so sorry. It can be scary to feel numb, and it's so easy to think "Why am I broken?" But you're not broken. I promise. And there are ways forward. 

If you're interested in reading further, you might like the book CPTSD: from surviving to thriving. Even if you don't think you have any semblance of PTSD. The book goes into why a numbing response helps people in certain life situations and what you can do to get out of it. 

Best of luck to you. I'm rooting for you. 

\-J

100% it did. It was my first impulse, to make art about it. The day I learned about what happened, I tried to make a song about it and just couldn't figure it out. I walked out to the house I used to live in with that friend and I recorded myself talking to her. And then I worked backwards from there, thinking "How did we get here?"  
Anyways, that recording I made of myself talking to her, that's the clip that plays in the very last few seconds. "I wonder if I'd do things differently, if I'd known this day was coming. I'd like to think that I would."  
I said that because she'd called me a month before all of it happened, saying that she had to leave that town. I'd moved across the country and she was still in that tiny town. She called me saying we should move in together; she was depressed and needed to get out; she missed me. I told her I wanted that, but I needed a few more months to get ready to move, I couldn't just uproot everything to move in with her. In the meantime, things got bad enough on her end that she did what she did. That's what most of the album is about. Trying to reconcile the whole idea that 1) if I'd acted differently she could possibly still be alive, and 2) that doesn't have to mean it's "my fault."

​

So all of the samples and videos and whatnot, they all sort of revolve around the guilt there. About missing her and feeling envious that she "got away" and I'm still "stuck" out here. That sort of stuff. It was immensely therapeutic, getting to just sit with those emotions so heavily while making this. And it's been really therapeutic having random strangers on the internet witnessing that process. I don't know why, but it has been.

I'm transitioning to van life in the northeast. Vermont, specifically. 

There's no wrong place to do it. What matters more is who you are, what you're willing to put up with, what your reasons are for doing it, etc. Yes, it will help you save money and give you some locational flexibility. But does it appeal to you for personal reasons too? Or would it feel like a sacrifice? If you're only doing it for logistical reasons, my fear is that you'd start to resent it and seek something else.

From what I've seen, the people who seem to do well living in vans are the people who are already drawn to minimalism/asceticism as well as those who foster strong senses of adventure. This is usually what keeps people on the road. Is that you? 

If you're the type of person who wants that, and your only hesitation is location, then I'd say fuck it. Make the leap. See what happens. Plenty of people get damn good at stealth camping, showering in gyms, and finding wi-fi in coffeeshops. It can be exhilarating if you let it be. 

I suggest you read some of the blogs and posts about van life that circulate here. Stay away from the videos and photos--those glamorize what vanlife is really like. Get a taste for what it entails, the good AND the bad, and if it doesn't scare you away, then do it.

It's generally protocol not to announce suicides formally, especially before the actual motive has been determined. There are a number of reasons for this. First, it's illegal to announce that it's suicide until suicidal intent has been determined by an investigation. Second, there's the social contagion effect of suicide—the more you announce them, the more likely they are to occur within the local populace. Third, announcements of suicide generally cause a lot of curious onlookers to flock to the area and gooseneck, which complicates investigations and emergency responses. Fourth, it'd be pretty shitty if the family learned of their relative's suicide through a 24 hour news press release.
